The problem: Liu marks at most n points, then Xiang marks at most n points (all distinct); the stick is cut at all marks; they alternately claim pieces, Liu first. For each n determine the largest c such that Liu can guarantee at least c.

Answer: c_n = 2^n/(2^(n+1)-1).

The write-up states this answer clearly: c(n) = 2^n/(2^{n+1}-1). So answer = 2.

Reduction (R): Lemma 1 proves that under optimal play, Liu obtains p_1 + p_3 + p_5 + ... where pieces are sorted in nonincreasing order. The proof is standard: Liu takes largest remaining, guaranteeing at least p_{2k-1} for his k-th piece; Xiang similarly holds Liu to at most that. This is a full proof of the reduction. So reduction = 2.

Lower bound (L): Liu marks points x_j = (2^j - 1)/D for j=1..n, giving blocks 1/D, 2/D, 4/D, ..., 2^n/D. Then Lemma 2 is used: for any further cutting at at most n points, there exist coefficients ε_i ∈ {-1,0,1} not all zero with |Σ ε_i a_i| ≤ Δ. Then since all nontrivial signed sums of powers of 2 divided by D are at least 1/D in absolute value (by uniqueness of binary representation), Δ ≥ 1/D, hence L = (1+Δ)/2 ≥ 2^n/D.

Graph construction: vertices are the n+1 blocks. For each pair of pieces (two pieces paired together in the sorted pairing), if they come from different blocks, join those vertices by an edge; if from same block, add a loop. G has n+1 vertices, at most n edges (one edge per pair, r ≤ n pairs). Wait—loops count as edges. With r ≤ n pairs, at most n edges including loops. Fine.

"A connected component containing a cycle or a loop has at least as many edges as vertices." Hmm, careful: a loop at a vertex contributes 1 edge and 1 to the degree of the vertex (2 in standard degree counting, but for edge count purposes a component with a loop and no other edges has 1 vertex, 1 edge — edges ≥ vertices? 1 ≥ 1, yes). A component with a cycle has edges ≥ vertices. Yes, that's standard for multigraphs (with loops counting as one edge). Since total edges ≤ n < n+1 = total vertices, some component T has fewer edges than vertices. Hence T is a tree (acyclic, no loops), possibly a single vertex.

"Every final piece coming from a block in T is represented either as an endpoint of an edge of T or as the unique leftover piece." Hmm, let me think. Each final piece belongs to some block. Pieces are paired; each pair corresponds to an edge (or loop). If a piece from a block v ∈ T is paired with a piece from a block outside T, the edge would leave T — but T is a connected component, so no edge joins a vertex of T to outside. If a piece from block v ∈ T is paired with another piece from the same block v, that would be a loop at v, but T is a tree (no loops). So all pieces from blocks in T are paired with pieces from other blocks in T, i.e., are endpoints of edges of T, except the leftover piece z if it lies in a block of T. Good.

For each vertex v ∈ T: a_v = Σ_{e∋v} w_{v,e} + z_v, where the sum is over edges of T incident to v and z_v is the leftover if it lies in v. This holds because all pieces of block v are accounted: each piece is either paired (edge incident to v in T) or the leftover. That edge joins v to u, crossing components — impossible since components are maximal. So indeed all pieces of blocks in T are endpoints of T's edges or the leftover. Good.

Bipartition: T is a tree, bipartite; signs σ_v ∈ {−1,+1} with adjacent opposite. S = Σ_{v∈T} σ_v a_v.
